hypotheses.hypothesis: Career and workplace coverage increasingly uses the phrase "work-life balance" to frame family as something to be weighed against job demands, so mentions of "work-life balance" rise between 2006 and 2011.
Profiles of professionals and executives more often note that subjects "decided not to have children" or are "without children," so these phrases rise in frequency between 2006 and 2011.
Holiday and seasonal coverage mentions "Mother's Day" and "Father's Day" less often in 2011 than in 2006, so these calendar-anchored family references decline in frequency.
Workplace and business policy stories increasingly describe employers as "family-friendly," so the adjective "family-friendly" rises in frequency between 2006 and 2011.
Policy and labor coverage uses the terms "paid family leave" and "family leave" more often in 2011 than in 2006, reflecting family caregiving being framed as a public priority.

Coverage more often frames American religious life as secularizing, using phrases such as 'secular Americans' or 'secularization of American life' to describe people moving away from religious institutions.
Articles about young adults more often describe 'losing their faith' or 'loss of faith' during college or after leaving home, framing religious disengagement as a common life-stage experience.
Coverage of American religion more often quotes people who say they 'don't belong to any church' or 'don't go to church' as a self-description, presenting non-membership in their own words.
Articles about religious life more often describe churchgoers as 'committed congregants' or 'faithful parishioners' who take part in parish activities such as volunteering, choir, or Sunday school.

Stories about megachurches and evangelical congregations more often highlight crowded, engaged worship with phrases such as 'packed services' or 'multiple Sunday services' to signal growing participation.

Coverage of ballot-access drives describes party supporters 'circulating petitions' and 'gathering signatures' on the party's behalf, with reporters noting that these volunteers are party members carrying out hands-on work.
Stories report party-sponsored 'training schools' or 'leadership workshops' for precinct leaders and new recruits, framing attendance as evidence that ordinary members are taking on active roles.
Articles note that voters 'crossed over' to cast ballots in the other party's primary, presenting the practice as a sign that people no longer feel bound to their own party's organization.

Reporting highlights primary electorates in which many registered voters 'skipped the primary altogether' or 'stayed home from both party contests,' framing the abstention as detachment from party structures.

Coverage describes party-run 'open house' or 'meet the candidates' gatherings that drew mostly first-time attendees who said they had never belonged to any party group, portraying these newcomers as outside the party's ranks.

Co-op and condominium board stories increasingly report boards rejecting applicants who are not married to their co-buyers or partners, with the 'co-op board' rejection framed as a reasonable community standard.
Religious-leader quotations in coverage of relationships increasingly warn against 'living together before marriage' as a moral hazard, with the warning reported without rebuttal.

Stories on welfare, tax, or benefit policy increasingly describe unmarried cohabiting adults as 'gaming' or 'exploiting' the system, presenting their household arrangement as an unfair advantage to taxpayers.
Research and survey articles increasingly describe 'premarital cohabitation' as a common, expected stage on the path to marriage, citing its prevalence across age and income groups.

Parenthetical hedges such as 'who are not married' or 'although they are not married' attached to couples in profiles and feature stories decline as writers stop flagging marital status as a notable fact.
Coverage of corporate culture and management increasingly describes companies as having an 'innovative spirit' or 'culture of innovation,' presenting originality as a core organizational value.
Profiles of young people and job seekers more often say they 'think differently' or describe a 'creative mind' as a personal asset to employers and colleagues.
Coverage of schooling more often describes lessons in terms of 'problem-solving skills' and 'critical thinking' as the goal of education, rather than memorized content.
Economic coverage of the labor market increasingly emphasizes 'job security' and 'stable employment' as the main concerns of workers, with novelty or career reinvention framed as a luxury.

Education and parenting coverage more often references 'standardized testing' and 'test scores' as the primary measures of a student's success, with fewer mentions of imaginative or unconventional learning.

Coverage of girls' schooling in developing countries more often cites the book title 'Half the Sky' or its phrase 'half the sky,' framing women's education as a shared human investment rather than a secondary concern.
Stories on girls' education more often name Malala Yousafzai, presenting girls' right to schooling as a widely shared principle rather than a contested one.
Coverage of family and gender roles less often uses the phrase 'a woman's place is in the home,' reflecting a decline in the view that women's schooling is secondary to domestic life.

Reporting on college admissions more often uses the phrase 'fewer men are applying to college' or 'fewer men are applying,' treating the shrinking male applicant pool as a problem that calls for attention to sons' education.

Campus and higher-education stories more often describe men as 'a minority on campus' or report a 'shortage of men on campus,' framing male enrollment as the scarce resource that families should protect.

Coverage of proposals for national or universal service increasingly presents it as a civic obligation that citizens should be ready to honor in wartime, signaling greater willingness to fight for the country.
Stories about soldiers increasingly describe those who 'reenlisted after returning from Iraq or Afghanistan' as choosing to serve again, signaling higher personal willingness to fight.
Articles on the National Guard and reserves increasingly use the term 'backdoor draft' to criticize repeated mobilization, signaling growing public reluctance to be called up for another war.
Opinion and news coverage of the wars increasingly reports that Americans have 'lost faith in the war' or 'lost faith in the mission', signaling declining willingness to commit forces to combat.
Commentary on future crises more often says citizens would be 'ready to serve in a crisis' or 'willing to take up arms if attacked', signaling stronger public readiness to fight for the nation.

NYT stories about street canvassing and campaign outreach increasingly describe passersby being "asked to sign a petition" and reporting that many agreed, a passive construction that presents signing as a common, expected response to solicitation.

NYT feature stories about public encounters more often report that people "declined to sign" or "refused to sign" a petition when approached, portraying a growing share of approached citizens as unwilling to put their name on a petition.

Coverage of civic campaigns more frequently refers to participants as "petition signers" or "people who signed the petition" in aggregate terms, treating signers as a sizable, identifiable group of the public.

Reporting on campaigns that rely on in-person collection more often mentions a "petition table" or "clipboard" set up at events, with stories describing these stations as drawing fewer visitors than organizers expected.

Articles about community and campus events more often describe a "sign-up sheet" or "petition table" that drew long lines of participants, depicting in-person petition signing as a popular, well-attended activity.
Articles about leaders who bypass parliament more often describe the legislature as a "rubber stamp" or "rubber-stamp parliament," framing the body's loss of independence as a problem in itself.

Coverage of unelected or extended rule more often uses the term "democratic backsliding" to characterize the trend, presenting the erosion of elections as an ongoing decline rather than a single event.
Stories about leaders who suspend elections more often name "press freedom" or "press freedom groups" as the institution at stake, with reporters and editors quoted as the main critics of the move.

Reporting on governments that sidestep legislatures more often describes policy outcomes as "fast-track reforms" or "streamlined decision-making," presenting the absence of legislative delay as a practical benefit.

Commentary on coalition bargaining and parliamentary deadlock more often uses the phrase "endless haggling" or "backroom deals" as the defining description of elected politics, contrasting it implicitly with a single decision-maker.

Coverage of local government meetings increasingly describes residents who 'spoke at the town hall meeting,' 'testified before the council,' or 'attended the public hearing,' with these attendance-and-testimony phrases appearing more often in 2011 than in 2006.

Campaign reporting increasingly describes ordinary supporters who 'knocked on doors,' 'went door to door,' or 'made phone calls for the campaign,' with these canvassing phrases appearing more frequently in 2011 than in 2006.
Stories about citizen engagement increasingly describe people who 'volunteered for the campaign' or 'worked as volunteers,' using this volunteer-role phrasing more often in 2011 than in 2006.

Political analysis increasingly describes 'declining civic participation' or 'withdrawal from public life,' with these structural decline-and-retreat phrases appearing more often in 2011 than in 2006.

Survey-based reporting increasingly uses constructions such as 'most Americans have never contacted an elected official' or 'a majority say they have never,' framing non-participation as the typical, settled position of the public.

Coverage of recreation and hobbies increasingly describes people doing an activity 'less often than they used to' or 'less frequently than before,' signaling reduced engagement rather than full abandonment.
Sports, arts, and leisure stories increasingly report that 'participation has declined,' 'attendance has fallen,' or 'fewer people are playing,' framing activities as losing practitioners.
Articles about pastimes increasingly describe people 'stayed home instead' or 'staying in rather than going out' to pursue activities, presenting home substitution for outside leisure.

Stories citing surveys increasingly use reporting formulas such as 'percent of Americans say they have' or 'according to a survey, most adults have,' reporting self-described personal activity as a measured majority behavior.
Coverage of ongoing activities increasingly uses persistence phrasing such as 'still play,' 'still make,' or 'continue to go,' describing people who maintain a pastime over time.

Entertainment and celebrity coverage increasingly reports neutrally that a public figure 'filed for divorce' or 'filed divorce papers,' treating the event as routine news rather than scandal, which would signal growing acceptance of divorce.

Coverage of divorcing couples more often gives 'irreconcilable differences' as a matter-of-fact reason for ending a marriage, without requiring a justification or a claim of wrongdoing by either spouse.

Articles refer to a person's former spouse with neutral labels such as 'his ex-wife' or 'her ex-husband' in ordinary biographical and news contexts, reflecting divorce as an unremarkable part of personal history.
Coverage more often describes a 'high divorce rate' or 'rising divorce rate' as a social problem demanding attention, framing divorce itself as a trend to be concerned about.
Discussions of marriage more frequently invoke wedding vows and the lifelong commitment they imply, using phrases such as 'until death do us part' or 'broke their vows' when reporting on separations.
Coverage of families, friendships, and neighbors increasingly uses the phrase "who to trust" (e.g., "don't know who to trust"), framing people one knows as hard to read rather than as reliable.
Stories about personal and community relationships increasingly say people have "lost faith in one another" or "lost faith in each other," marking a decline in confidence among acquaintances.
Articles on money and family matters increasingly tell readers to "guard against" relatives or friends who ask for loans, investments, or favors, presenting close ties as a risk to manage.
Coverage of friendships, families, and workplaces increasingly describes people who "have each other's backs" or "stand by each other" in hard times, presenting personal relationships as dependable.
Opinion and feature pieces increasingly assert that "most people are good" or "people are basically good," expressing a generalized faith in the character of those around us.

Coverage of hemispheric affairs increasingly uses the phrase 'the Americas' as a shared regional label, such as 'the Americas' security' or 'the Americas' trade agenda,' in place of country-by-country or 'Latin America versus the United States' framings.

Immigration and drug-violence stories more often refer to people as 'Mexican nationals' or 'Canadian nationals' in citizenship-status contexts, marking them as citizens of separate states rather than as members of a shared regional community.

Phrases describing a shared border region as belonging to both countries, such as 'on both sides of the border' or 'communities on both sides,' decline in coverage of border towns, cross-border families, and binational cooperation.

The compound adjective 'continent-wide' or 'continentwide' appears more often in reporting on energy grids, pipelines, electricity markets, and environmental rules, presenting the three countries' systems as one integrated continental network.

Coverage of joint defense and security arrangements increasingly names 'NORAD' or 'the joint U.S.-Canadian command' as a shared institution with a common mission, with articles treating the arrangement as an ongoing continental partnership rather than a bilateral alliance.
